'''Deji Akinwande''' is a [[Nigerian-American]] professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering with courtesy affiliation with Materials Science, and Biomedical Engineering at the [[University of Texas at Austin]].<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |title=Deji Akinwande {{!}} Texas ECE - Electrical & Computer Engineering at UT Austin |url=https://www.ece.utexas.edu/people/faculty/deji-akinwande |access-date=2022-02-28 |website=www.ece.utexas.edu}}</ref> He was awarded the [[Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers]] in 2016 from [[Barack Obama]].<ref name=":7" /> He is a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]], the [[African Academy of Sciences]], the [[Materials Research Society]] (MRS), and the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers|IEEE]].

== Early life and education ==
Akinwande was born in [[Washington, D.C.|Washington, DC]] and moved to [[Nigeria]] in his early years.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://zodml.org/discover-nigeria/people/deji-akinwande#.W937cRP7Tx4|title=Deji Akinwande|website=ZODML|access-date=2018-11-03|archive-date=2018-11-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181104011819/https://zodml.org/discover-nigeria/people/deji-akinwande#.W937cRP7Tx4|url-status=dead}}</ref> He grew up in [[Ikeja]] with his parents.<ref name=":0" /> His father was the financial controller of [[Guardian News]] and his mother worked at the Ministry of Education. He attended [[Federal Government College, Idoani]] and became interested in science and engineering.<ref name=":0" /> He returned to America in 1994, starting at Cuyahoga community college and eventually transferring to [[Case Western Reserve University]] to study electrical engineering and applied physics.<ref name=":0" /> During his master's degree he pioneered the design of near-field microwave tips for non-destructive imaging.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://eds.ieee.org/publications/631-deji-akinwande|title=Deji Akinwande|website=[[IEEE]]|access-date=2018-11-03|archive-date=2018-11-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181104010426/https://eds.ieee.org/publications/631-deji-akinwande|url-status=dead}}</ref> He was accepted to [[Stanford University]] as a graduate student, working on the electronic properties of carbon-based materials.<ref name=":0" /> He was selected as an [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]] Fellow during his PhD.<ref name=":0" /> He was also selected as a DARE (Diversifying Academia, Recruiting Excellence) Fellow in 2008.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news.stanford.edu/2018/11/01/stanford-sows-seeds-diversity-academia-phd-fellowships/|title=Sowing seeds of diversity in academia with PhD fellowships|last=University|first=Stanford|date=2018-11-01|work=Stanford News|access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref> He completed his PhD in 2009.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://gradlogic.org/akinwande-intrvw/|title=People and Ideas {{!}} Interview with Deji Akinwande|date=2016-04-12|work=GRAD {{!}} LOGIC|access-date=2018-11-03|archive-date=2021-10-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211026120846/http://gradlogic.org/akinwande-intrvw/|url-status=dead}}</ref> He joined [[University of Texas at Austin]] in 2010 as an Assistant Professor in January 2010, and was awarded research grants from several agencies including the National Science Foundation (NSF), Army Research Office (ARO), the Defense Threat Reduction Agency (DTRA), DARPA, AFOSR, and [[Office of Naval Research]], the latter focusing on high-frequency flexible 2D electronics.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|url=http://www.ece.utexas.edu/news/prof-akinwande-awarded-grant-onr|title=Prof. Akinwande Awarded Grant from ONR|date=2013-05-31|work=Texas ECE {{!}} Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering {{!}} The University of Texas at Austin|access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref>

== Research and career ==
Akinwande collaborated with [[Aixtron]] on wafer-scale growth of graphene, characterization and integration <ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aixtron.com/en/investors/The%20University%20of%20Texas%20at%20Austin%20orders%20AIXTRON%20Black%20Magic%20for%20wearable%20electronics%20project_n351|title=AIXTRON SE Investor Relations − An Investment with a Future :: AIXTRON|website=aixtron.com|access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref> The collaboration demonstrated scalable growth of polycrystalline graphene using [[chemical vapor deposition]], creating the first 300&nbsp;mm wafers.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nano.mer.utexas.edu/2014/10/300mm-wafer-scale-graphene-demonstrated/|title=300mm wafer-scale graphene demonstrated {{!}} Akinwande Nano Research Group|website=nano.mer.utexas.edu|date=8 October 2014 |access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rahimi|first1=Somayyeh|last2=Tao|first2=Li|last3=Chowdhury|first3=Sk. Fahad|last4=Park|first4=Saungeun|last5=Jouvray|first5=Alex|last6=Buttress|first6=Simon|last7=Rupesinghe|first7=Nalin|last8=Teo|first8=Ken|last9=Akinwande|first9=Deji|date=2014-09-15|title=Toward 300 mm Wafer-Scalable High-Performance Polycrystalline Chemical Vapor Deposited Graphene Transistors|journal=ACS Nano|volume=8|issue=10|pages=10471–10479|doi=10.1021/nn5038493|pmid=25198884|s2cid=5077855 |issn=1936-0851}}</ref> In 2011 he published the first textbook on Carbon Nanotube and Graphene Device Physics with Prof. Philip Wong of Stanford University.<ref>{{Citation|last1=Wong|first1=H.-S. Philip|pages=47–72|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9780511778124|last2=Akinwande|first2=Deji|doi=10.1017/cbo9780511778124.004|title=Carbon Nanotube and Graphene Device Physics|year=2010}}</ref> He was made a senior member of [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE) in 2013.<ref name=":1" /> He has made several advances in two dimensional graphene electronics.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Akinwande|first1=Deji|last2=Petrone|first2=Nicholas|last3=Hone|first3=James|date=December 2014|title=Two-dimensional flexible nanoelectronics|journal=Nature Communications|volume=5|issue=1|pages=5678|doi=10.1038/ncomms6678|pmid=25517105|issn=2041-1723|bibcode=2014NatCo...5.5678A|doi-access=free}}</ref> In 2015 he demonstrated the first two dimensional [[silicene]] transistor.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Tao|first1=Li|last2=Cinquanta|first2=Eugenio|last3=Chiappe|first3=Daniele|last4=Grazianetti|first4=Carlo|last5=Fanciulli|first5=Marco|last6=Dubey|first6=Madan|last7=Molle|first7=Alessandro|last8=Akinwande|first8=Deji|s2cid=5144735|date=2015-02-02|title=Silicene field-effect transistors operating at room temperature|journal=Nature Nanotechnology|volume=10|issue=3|pages=227–231|doi=10.1038/nnano.2014.325|pmid=25643256|issn=1748-3387|bibcode=2015NatNa..10..227T|hdl=10281/84255|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Akinwande in collaboration with Alessandro Molle's group at CNR, Italy, achieved this by evaporating silicon onto a crystal of silver, monitoring the growth in real-time using [[Scanning tunneling microscope|scanning tunnelling microscopy]].<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Peplow|first=Mark|date=2015-02-02|title=Graphene's cousin silicene makes transistor debut|journal=Nature|volume=518|issue=7537|pages=17–18|doi=10.1038/518017a|pmid=25652975|issn=0028-0836|bibcode=2015Natur.518...17P|doi-access=free}}</ref> This research breakthrough was selected as one of the top science stories of 2015 by [[Discover (magazine)|Discover magazine]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.ece.utexas.edu/news/prof-akinwandes-silicene-transistor-named-discover-top-100-story-2015|title=Prof. Akinwande's Silicene Transistor Named Discover Top 100 Story of 2015|date=2015-12-18|work=Texas ECE {{!}} Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering {{!}} The University of Texas at Austin|access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref> The silicene work was the most cited [[Nature Nanotechnology]] publication of similar age.

He went on to demonstrate the thinnest most transparent electronic tattoo sensors made from [[graphene]] in 2017, which were less than 500&nbsp;nm thick and 85% optically transparent. This research was in collaboration with [[Nanshu Lu]]'s group.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Kabiri Ameri|first1=Shideh|last2=Ho|first2=Rebecca|last3=Jang|first3=Hongwoo|last4=Tao|first4=Li|last5=Wang|first5=Youhua|last6=Wang|first6=Liu|last7=Schnyer|first7=David M.|last8=Akinwande|first8=Deji|last9=Lu|first9=Nanshu|s2cid=19751409|date=2017-07-27|title=Graphene Electronic Tattoo Sensors|journal=ACS Nano|volume=11|issue=8|pages=7634–7641|doi=10.1021/acsnano.7b02182|pmid=28719739|issn=1936-0851}}</ref> The tattoos can be laminated onto human skin like a [[temporary tattoo]], but could measure [[electrocardiography]], [[electroencephalography]], temperature and hydration.<ref name=":4" /> Subsequently, the graphene tattoos were developed as a wearable platform for monitoring blood pressure continuously using the bio-impedance modality published in Nature Nanotechnology in 2022.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kireev |first1=Dmitry |last2=Sel |first2=Kaan |last3=Ibrahim |first3=Bassem |last4=Kumar |first4=Neelotpala |last5=Akbari |first5=Ali |last6=Jafari |first6=Roozbeh |last7=Akinwande |first7=Deji |date=2022-06-20 |title=Continuous cuffless monitoring of arterial blood pressure via graphene bioimpedance tattoos |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41565-022-01145-w |journal=Nature Nanotechnology |volume=17 |issue=8 |language=en |pages=864–870 |doi=10.1038/s41565-022-01145-w |pmid=35725927 |bibcode=2022NatNa..17..864K |s2cid=249873611 |issn=1748-3395|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He demonstrated the first [[atomristor]] by investigating [[Volatile memory|nonvolatile]] resistance switching using a 2D atomic sheet of [[molybdenum disulfide]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ge|first1=Ruijing|last2=Wu|first2=Xiaohan|last3=Kim|first3=Myungsoo|last4=Shi|first4=Jianping|last5=Sonde|first5=Sushant|last6=Tao|first6=Li|last7=Zhang|first7=Yanfeng|last8=Lee|first8=Jack C.|last9=Akinwande|first9=Deji|date=2017-12-19|title=Atomristor: Nonvolatile Resistance Switching in Atomic Sheets of Transition Metal Dichalcogenides|journal=Nano Letters|volume=18|issue=1|pages=434–441|doi=10.1021/acs.nanolett.7b04342|pmid=29236504|issn=1530-6984|doi-access=free|bibcode=2018NanoL..18..434G}}</ref> Remarkably, the memory effect persists down to a single atom.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hus |first1=Saban M. |last2=Ge |first2=Ruijing |last3=Chen |first3=Po-An |last4=Liang |first4=Liangbo |last5=Donnelly |first5=Gavin E. |last6=Ko |first6=Wonhee |last7=Huang |first7=Fumin |last8=Chiang |first8=Meng-Hsueh |last9=Li |first9=An-Ping |last10=Akinwande |first10=Deji |date=January 2021 |title=Observation of single-defect memristor in an MoS2 atomic sheet |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41565-020-00789-w |journal=Nature Nanotechnology |language=en |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=58–62 |doi=10.1038/s41565-020-00789-w |pmid=33169008 |s2cid=226285710 |issn=1748-3395|arxiv=2002.01574 }}</ref> The devices can be as thin as 1.5&nbsp;nm and have applications in [[5G]] and future 6G<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2022-05-30 |title=Towards zero-power 6G communication switches using atomic sheets |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41928-022-00767-1 |journal=Nature Electronics |volume=5 |issue=6 |language=en |pages=331–332 |doi=10.1038/s41928-022-00767-1 |s2cid=249221166 |issn=2520-1131|url-access=subscription }}</ref> smartphones as zero-static power radio-frequency switches, [[internet of things]] and [[artificial intelligence]] circuits.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.engr.utexas.edu/news/8289-ultra-thin-memory-storage|title=Ultra-Thin Memory Storage Device Paves Way for More Powerful Computing - Cockrell School of Engineering|last=Wunderlich|first=Rebecca|website=engr.utexas.edu|date=18 January 2018 |access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref> The discovery of memory in these systems is expected to be universal amongst 2D materials.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/96/i3/Two-dimensional-materials-enable-low.html|title=Two-dimensional materials could enable low-power telecommunications {{!}} January 15, 2018 Issue - Vol. 96 Issue 3 {{!}} Chemical & Engineering News|last=Bourzac|first=Katherine|website=cen.acs.org|access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref>

He was on the Board of Reviewing Editors for Science, an associate editor of ACS Nano, a past editor for Nature journal npj 2D Materials and Applications, and a past editor of [[IEEE Electron Devices Society|IEEE Electron Devices]] Letters.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://eds.ieee.org/publications/electron-device-letters/editor-in-chief-and-editors|title=EDL Editor-in-Chief and Editors|website=[[IEEE]]|access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nature.com/npj2dmaterials/about/editor|title=About the Editor {{!}} npj 2D Materials and Applications|website=nature.com|access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref> He has given more than a dozen plenary and keynote talks including the plenary talk at the 2017 [[SPIE]] annual meeting Optics & Photonics, where he discussed the progress, opportunities and challenges of [[2D Material|2D]] electronic devices, and the Kavli plenary at the MRS Fall in Boston Dec. 2024.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=http://spie.org/newsroom/op17_akinwande_2d-flexible-and-emerging-devices-and-applications?SSO=1|title=2D Flexible and Emerging Devices and Applications {{!}} SPIE Homepage: SPIE|website=spie.org|access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref> He was made an [[American Physical Society]] Fellow in 2017 and a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright]] Fellow in 2018.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.ece.utexas.edu/about/awards/akinwande-aps-2017|title=Akinwande-APS-2017|date=2017-10-11|work=Texas ECE {{!}} Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering {{!}} The University of Texas at Austin|access-date=2018-11-03|archive-date=2018-01-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180126102807/http://www.ece.utexas.edu/about/awards/akinwande-aps-2017|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.ece.utexas.edu/news/prof-deji-akinwande-elected-fellow-american-physical-society|title=Prof. Deji Akinwande Elected Fellow of the American Physical Society|date=2017-10-19|work=Texas ECE {{!}} Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering {{!}} The University of Texas at Austin|access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref> He visited the [[Adam Mickiewicz University in Poznań]] in 2019 as a Fulbright Specialist Fellow.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://en.fulbright.edu.pl/current-american-grantees/|title=2018-2019 American Grantees {{!}} Polsko-Amerykańska Komisja Fulbrighta|work=Polsko-Amerykańska Komisja Fulbrighta|access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref> Three of his former postdoctoral scholars are now professors, Dr. Shideh Kabiri at [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]] in [[Canada]], Dr. Li Tao at [[Southeast University]] in [[Nanjing]], and Dr. Seongin Hong at Gachon University. Myungsoo Kim, a former PhD student is now a Professor at [[Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology|UNIST]] in South Korea.

He was a finalist for the [[University of Texas at Austin]] 'UT System Regents’ Outstanding Teaching' Award for several years, the highest teaching recognition in Texas.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2016-03-11 |title=Deji Akinwande - World Class Researcher; Creating Solutions in Science and Technology. |work=Konnect Africa |url=https://www.konnectafrica.net/deji-akinwande-world-class-researcher-creating-solutions-in-science-and-technology/ |access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref>

He has chaired several major conferences and program committees in nanoelectronics/nanotechnology such as:
*[[Gordon Research Conference]] on 2D materials
*Device Research Conference
*the [[International Electron Devices Meeting]] NDT Sub-committee

==Academic posts==
*Cockrell Family Regents Chair in Engineering #8, UT-Austin 2023–Present
*Temple Foundation Endowed Professorship, UT-Austin 2020–2023
*Theodore von Kármán Fellow and visiting professor, [[RWTH Aachen University]], 2017
*Visiting professor, [[Cambridge University]] Engineering Department, and Fellow of [[Pembroke College, Cambridge]], 2016 
*Visiting scholar, CNR, Agrate Brianza, Italy, 2016

==Publications and patents==
*He has authored over 340 publications which have been cited over 33,000 times <ref>{{Cite web |title=Deji Akinwande |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ln3X8B0AAAAJ&hl=en |access-date=2024-11-12 |website=scholar.google.com}}</ref>
*He has published 1 textbook and 3 book chapters
*He has delivered over a dozen plenary and keynote talks
*He has given more than 130 invited talks and seminars at conferences, universities and institutions
*He has 6 patents awarded or pending covering inventions in electronics and nanotechnology
